title: Review: Balanced equations and reacting masses; Molar gas volume and Avogadro's law; Limiting reagent and yield; Atom economy; Titrations and solution calculations
source: Questions copied unchanged from the mission-lesson scripts for AQA A-level Chemistry (status of the source: mission-lesson scripts of Oct-Nov 2026 (reviewed by AI reviewers; not signed off by a person)). Terms and clues: AM08#t2 term and clue written for the game; AM05#t2 term and clue written for the game; AM08#t1 term and clue written for the game; AM09#t1 term and clue written for the game. Questions: AM05#N.10b, AM07#N.6a, AM08#N.6a, AM09#N.6, AM10#N.9, AM05#N.7b, AM07#N.4a, AM08#N.9, AM09#N.4a, AM10#N.3, AM05#N.4, AM07#N.14. Some questions repeat from the worlds it reviews.

assemble.prompt: Match each term to its definition.

items.label: Conical flask
items.clue: Vessel in which the two solutions meet, swirled over a white tile.

items.label: Coefficient
items.clue: A number in a balanced equation; for gases these give the reacting volume ratio.

items.label: Indicator
items.clue: A few drops are added so a visible change shows when the moles match the equation.

items.label: Limiting reactant
items.clue: The starting substance used up first, which fixes the maximum quantity of product.

questions.stem: Two identical 500 cm³ flasks are at 25 °C and 1.00 × 10⁵ Pa. One is filled with neon, Ne, and one with sulfur hexafluoride, SF₆, a dense gas used in electrical switchgear. The SF₆ flask holds 7.2 times the mass of gas. Which statement is correct? (R = 8.31 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹; Ar: F 19.0, Ne 20.2, S 32.1)

options.text: Each flask holds 2.02 × 10⁻² mol of gas.
Each flask holds 2.41 × 10⁻¹ mol of gas.
Each flask holds 20.2 mol of gas.
The neon flask holds 2.02 × 10⁻² mol, the SF₆ flask 2.79 × 10⁻³ mol.

questions.explanation: n = pV/RT = (1.00 × 10⁵ × 5.00 × 10⁻⁴) ÷ (8.31 × 298) = 2.02 × 10⁻² mol. Nothing in pV = nRT depends on which gas it is.

questions.stem: Magnesium ribbon fizzes and dissolves in dilute hydrochloric acid. Which is the ionic equation for the reaction?
questions.explanation: Cl⁻ is a spectator. 1 Mg and 2 H each side; charge 2+ each side.

questions.stem: Vinegar (ethanoic acid, a weak acid) is in the conical flask. Sodium hydroxide is added from the burette. Which indicator should be used, and what is the colour change at the end point?

options.text: Methyl orange, from red to yellow
Either indicator, because the acid and alkali react in a 1 : 1 ratio

questions.explanation: Weak acid + strong base: phenolphthalein. It is colourless in the acid and turns pink when a slight excess of alkali is present.

questions.stem: Which statement describes the theoretical yield of a product in a reaction?

options.text: The mass of product actually obtained at the end of the experiment
The total mass of all the reactants put in, since mass is conserved
The mass of product calculated from the amount of the limiting reactant
The mass of product calculated from the reactant with the smaller number of moles

questions.explanation: The theoretical yield is the maximum mass of product, from the limiting reactant and the mole ratio, assuming complete reaction and no losses.

questions.stem: Hydrogen is manufactured by reacting methane with steam: CH₄(g) + H₂O(g) → CO(g) + 3H₂(g). In one batch, 16.0 kg of methane gave 4.80 kg of hydrogen. What is the atom economy for producing hydrogen by this reaction? (Aᵣ: H 1.0, C 12.0, O 16.0)
questions.explanation: 3 × 2.0 ÷ (16.0 + 18.0) × 100 = 6.0 ÷ 34.0 × 100 = 17.6%. The products total is the same: 28.0 + 6.0 = 34.0. The rest of the mass ends up as CO.

questions.stem: Magnesium reacts with excess dilute hydrochloric acid: Mg(s) + 2HCl(aq) → MgCl₂(aq) + H₂(g). What volume of hydrogen, in cm³, forms from 0.120 g of magnesium at 20 °C and 1.01 × 10⁵ Pa? (Ar: Mg 24.3; R = 8.31 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹)
Aluminium burns in oxygen to form aluminium oxide. Which equation for this reaction is correctly balanced?
questions.explanation: Al₂O₃ and O₂ are the right formulae. 3O₂ gives 6 O = 2Al₂O₃, which needs 4Al. 4 Al and 6 O each side.

questions.stem: A student records these titres: 24.30 cm³ (rough), 23.85 cm³, 23.40 cm³ and 23.50 cm³. Which mean titre should be used in the calculation?
questions.explanation: Only 23.40 and 23.50 cm³ are concordant (within 0.10 cm³). Their mean is 23.45 cm³.

questions.stem: Nitrogen and hydrogen react: N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) → 2NH₃(g). A mixture contains 5.60 g of N₂ and 1.50 g of H₂. Which statement is correct? (Aᵣ: H 1.0, N 14.0)

options.text: H₂ is limiting, because a smaller mass of H₂ is present.
H₂ is limiting, because the equation needs three times as much H₂ as N₂.
H₂ is limiting: 0.750 mol H₂ needs 2.25 mol N₂, and only 0.200 mol N₂ is present.
N₂ is limiting: 0.200 mol N₂ needs 0.600 mol H₂, and 0.750 mol H₂ is present.

questions.explanation: n(N₂) = 5.60 ÷ 28.0 = 0.200 mol; n(H₂) = 1.50 ÷ 2.0 = 0.750 mol. N₂ needs 3 × 0.200 = 0.600 mol H₂, which is available, so N₂ runs out first.

questions.stem: Which statement about atom economy and waste in an industrial process is correct?

options.text: The higher the percentage yield, the higher the atom economy, so less waste is produced.
Atom economy counts one molecule of each substance, so the coefficients do not affect it.
A process with an atom economy of 100% produces no waste of any kind at all.
The lower the atom economy, the greater the proportion of reactant mass that becomes waste.

questions.explanation: The mass not in the desired product ends up in by-products, so atom economy and waste are inversely related.

questions.stem: Sulfur dioxide reacts with oxygen: 2SO₂(g) + O₂(g) → 2SO₃(g). What volume of oxygen reacts completely with 30.0 cm³ of sulfur dioxide? All volumes are measured at the same temperature and pressure.
questions.explanation: Same T and p, so volumes are in the coefficient ratio: 30.0 × 1/2 = 15.0 cm³.

questions.stem: A strip of magnesium burns brightly in air and leaves white magnesium oxide: 2Mg(s) + O₂(g) → 2MgO(s). What mass of MgO forms from 2.43 g of Mg? (Ar: O 16.0, Mg 24.3)
